title: Pregnancy, postpartum and menopause
goal: Summarise guideline-based exercise advice in pregnancy, the evidence on postpartum return to running, and what is known about perimenopause and menopause for endurance athletes.

steps.title: Pregnancy: the Canadian guideline
steps.text:
The 2019 Canadian guideline is a [consensus statement](g:consensus-statement) built on a [systematic review](g:systematic-review). Without [contraindications](g:contraindication), being active in pregnancy goes with fewer newborn complications (babies born too large) and lower risks of gestational diabetes, high blood pressure disorders, caesarean section and depression, and with no link to miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth [[c:fem-preg-benefit]].

Women who were active before pregnancy may continue, adjusting as it advances [[c:fem-preg-continue]]. A [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) found 24% lower odds of [instrumental delivery](g:instrumental-delivery) in women who exercised, with no [dose-response](g:dose-response) [[c:fem-preg-sr]]. A list of absolute and relative contraindications exists: check it with an obstetric care provider.

claims.text: Without contraindications, prenatal physical activity is linked to fewer newborn complications and lower maternal risks, and not to miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth.

evidence.quote: fewer newborn complications (i.e., large for gestational age)
decreased risk of preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, Caesarean section, instrumental delivery, urinary incontinence, excessive gestational weight gain, and depression
Physical activity is not associated with miscarriage, stillbirth, neonatal death, preterm birth

claims.text: Previously active women may continue physical activity throughout pregnancy, modifying it as pregnancy progresses.

evidence.quote: Previously active women may continue physical activity throughout pregnancy.
Women may need to modify physical activity as pregnancy progresses.

claims.text: Prenatal exercise lowered the odds of instrumental delivery by 24%, with no dose-response across frequency, intensity, duration or volume.

evidence.quote: 'Moderate' quality evidence from exercise-only randomised controlled trials (RCTs) indicated a 24% reduction in the odds of instrumental delivery in women who exercised compared with women who did not
Results from meta-regression did not identify a dose-response relationship between frequency, intensity, duration or volume of exercise and labour and delivery outcomes.

steps.title: Intensity, and what is unknown at the top
steps.text:
The guideline defines moderate intensity as hard enough to noticeably raise heart rate, where you can talk but not sing. Brisk walking, stationary cycling at moderate effort and resistance training all count [[c:fem-preg-intensity]].

More activity generally brings more benefit, but the guideline found **no evidence on safety or extra benefit** well above its recommendations [[c:fem-preg-above]]. For a trained endurance athlete that is the gap: not shown to be harmful, but not studied. Where evidence is thin, the plan is individual and made with the obstetric care provider, and it changes as pregnancy goes on.

claims.text: Moderate intensity means a person can talk but not sing; examples include brisk walking, moderate stationary cycling and resistance training.

evidence.quote: intense enough to noticeably increase heart rate; a person can talk but not sing during activities of this intensity
stationary cycling (moderate effort), resistance training

claims.text: No evidence was found on the safety or extra benefit of exercise at levels well above the guideline recommendations.

evidence.quote: evidence was not identified regarding the safety or additional benefit of exercising at levels significantly above the recommendations

steps.title: Postpartum return to running
steps.text:
There is little evidence to guide elite athletes who want to return to competition after giving birth [[c:fem-pp-evidence]]. A clinical review (level 4 evidence) proposes a team-based plan that monitors [pelvic floor](g:pelvic-floor) and core function, progressive reloading of bone, muscle and tendon, nutrition, and [lactation](g:lactation) care if breastfeeding [[c:fem-pp-return]]. Return is 'highly individualized', not a set number of weeks.

Two links to earlier lessons: [low energy availability](g:low-energy-availability) matters when nursing and training ([REDs](g:reds) lessons), and a woman is not eumenorrheic just because she uses no contraception: the time cycles take to return varies widely [[c:fem-pp-cycle]].

claims.text: There is little evidence to guide elite athletes returning to competition after childbirth.

evidence.quote: There is little evidence to guide elite athletes who desire returning to competition after giving birth to a child.

claims.text: Return to running postpartum is individual and needs monitoring of nutrition, core and pelvic floor function, bone, muscle and tendon reloading, and breastfeeding care.

evidence.quote: Return to running in the postpartum period is a highly individualized process that benefits from multidisciplinary, individualized care.
This includes monitoring of nutrition, core and pelvic floor function, bone reloading, muscle and tendon reloading, and breastfeeding care when applicable.

claims.text: The time for eumenorrheic cycles to resume after childbirth varies considerably between women, so absence of contraception does not mean a normal cycle.

evidence.quote: Consider the timescale for resumption of eumenorrheic cycles following childbirth (i.e., in the postpartum period), given that this varies considerably between women

steps.title: Perimenopause and menopause
steps.text:
[Perimenopause](g:perimenopause) is when the ovaries gradually make less oestrogen. [Menopause](g:menopause) is when menstruation stops; post-menopause starts after 12 months without a period [[c:fem-meno-def]].

In an online survey of 187 female endurance athletes aged 40–60, sleep problems (88%), exhaustion (83%), anxiety (72%) and hot flushes (65%) were common. Joint and muscle discomfort, weight gain, sleep problems and exhaustion hurt training most [[c:fem-meno-symptoms]]. Respondents chose themselves, so rates may not fit all athletes.

Bone and muscle loss is fastest in this transition, yet few exercise trials included these women, and the six found were low quality [[c:fem-meno-bone]]. The masters-athlete lessons carry on from here.

claims.text: Perimenopause is the time when the ovaries gradually produce less oestrogen; post-menopause is the time after 12 consecutive months without periods.

evidence.quote: Define peri-menopause as the time around the occurrence of the menopause when the ovaries gradually produce less oestrogen
Define post-menopause as the time after which a woman has experienced 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea

claims.text: Menopausal symptoms are common in female endurance athletes aged 40–60; sleep problems, exhaustion, hot flushes and joint and muscle discomfort were among the most frequent.

evidence.quote: The most commonly reported menopausal symptoms were sleep problems (88%), physical and mental exhaustion (83%), sexual problems (74%), anxiety (72%), irritability (68%), depressive mood (67%), weight gain (67%), hot flushes (65%), and joint and muscular discomfort (63%).
The symptoms that were perceived to most negatively affect training and performance were joint and muscular discomfort, weight gain, sleep problems, and physical and mental exhaustion.

claims.text: Bone and muscle loss is fastest in the menopause transition, but most exercise trials left these women out, and the few that included them are low quality.

evidence.quote: The highest rate of bone and muscle loss occurs during the menopause transition.
Yet, most clinical exercise trials have excluded peri- and early post-menopausal female participants.
All studies had low quality of evidence, and high risk of bias.
Strength training and walking benefited total body, hip, spine, femoral neck, and trochanter aBMD and lean mass during early post-menopause.

points: The 2019 Canadian guideline supports exercise in pregnancy for women without contraindications, with no link to miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth.
Moderate intensity means you can talk but not sing; the safety of training far above the guideline levels is unstudied, so plan it individually.
Postpartum return to running is individual and monitors pelvic floor, core, load, nutrition and lactation; evidence is thin.
Menopausal symptoms are common in endurance athletes and can hurt training; trial evidence on bone and muscle is scarce and low quality.

variants.stem: According to the 2019 Canadian guideline, how is physical activity in pregnancy linked to miscarriage?

options.text: It is not associated with miscarriage
options.why: Right: the guideline found no link to miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth.

options.text: It raises the risk of miscarriage
options.why: The guideline found no such link.

options.text: It halves the risk of miscarriage
options.why: No protective effect on miscarriage was reported.

options.text: It raises the risk only for vigorous exercise
options.why: The guideline found no link, and no evidence on very high levels.

variants.stem: A healthy runner finds she is 6 weeks pregnant. She runs five days a week and has no contraindications. What does the guideline support?

options.text: Continue, adjusting as pregnancy advances
options.why: Right, with her care provider: previously active women may continue and adjust.

options.text: Stop all running until after birth
options.why: The guideline supports staying active for women without contraindications.

options.text: Switch to walking only
options.why: Moderate activity such as running at a talking pace is not ruled out.

options.text: Keep the same load all the way through
options.why: The guideline says women may need to modify activity as pregnancy progresses.

variants.stem: A pregnant cyclist rides at an effort where she can talk but not sing. Under the guideline, how is this effort described?

options.text: Moderate intensity
options.why: Right: talk but not sing marks moderate intensity.

options.text: Vigorous intensity
options.why: Vigorous effort would make talking hard.

options.text: Light intensity
options.why: Light effort would let her sing.

options.text: Unsafe
options.why: The guideline counts moderate cycling as an example of suitable activity.

variants.stem: A pregnant elite triathlete asks whether 12 hours of training a week is safe. What does the guideline allow you to say?

options.text: It was not studied; decide with her provider
options.why: Right: safety well above its recommendations was not studied, so the evidence gap is the honest answer.

options.text: The guideline proved such volumes safe
options.why: No evidence was found on safety at those levels.

options.text: The guideline showed harm above its recommendations
options.why: No harm was shown; it simply had no evidence.

options.text: Elite fitness removes any risk
options.why: Fitness is not covered, and no evidence shows this.

variants.stem: A runner is 8 weeks postpartum, breastfeeding and feeling fine. She wants to restart 40 km a week. Which plan fits the review best?

options.text: Progressive reloading with pelvic floor and core checks
options.why: Right: reload step by step and monitor these areas, including fuelling for lactation.

options.text: Return to full volume as soon as she feels fine
options.why: Feeling fine does not show pelvic floor or bone readiness.

options.text: Wait a fixed 12 weeks, then resume full training
options.why: The review calls return individual, not a set date followed by full volume.

options.text: Avoid running until weaning
options.why: The review does not ask for this; it adds lactation care to the plan.

variants.stem: Six months postpartum and using no contraception, a woman says her cycle is back to normal because she bled twice. A study wants to class her as eumenorrheic. What is missing?

options.text: Confirmation of ovulation and the hormone profile, as bleeding alone does not show them
options.why: Right: return of normal cycles varies and needs checking.

options.text: Nothing: no contraception means a normal cycle
options.why: Cycles return at different times, so this is an assumption.

options.text: A pregnancy test only
options.why: This does not show ovulation or the hormone profile.

options.text: Her age, as cycles return at the same time for everyone
options.why: Timing varies considerably between women.

variants.stem: How strong is the evidence for postpartum return-to-running programmes for elite athletes, according to the review?

options.text: Little: advice rests on best available evidence and clinical experience
options.why: Right: the review is level 4 evidence.

options.text: Strong: many randomised trials set the timetable
options.why: The review says there is little evidence.

options.text: Moderate: cohort studies give a clear week count
options.why: No fixed week count is given.

options.text: None is needed, as return follows the pre-birth plan
options.why: The review stresses an individual, monitored return.

variants.stem: How does the research guide define post-menopause?

options.text: 12 consecutive months without a period
options.why: Right: after a full year of amenorrhoea.

options.text: The first irregular period after age 40
options.why: Irregular periods mark the transition, not post-menopause.

options.text: The time when oestrogen starts to fall
options.why: This describes perimenopause.

options.text: 3 missed periods in a row
options.why: Three missed periods is the definition of secondary amenorrhoea.

variants.stem: A 52-year-old cyclist has night sweats, poor sleep and irregular periods, and her power has dropped. What is a sensible first step?

options.text: Log symptoms and discuss menopause with a doctor
options.why: Right: menopausal symptoms may be the cause; such symptoms are common in athletes and affect training.

options.text: Push harder, since more training will fix it
options.why: Poor sleep and exhaustion call for a cause, not more load.

options.text: Accept that fitness is gone with age
options.why: Age alone does not explain the drop; her symptoms may.

options.text: Stop all training to rule out overtraining
options.why: Nothing supports a full stop, and activity helps health.

variants.stem: The survey found 65% of 187 athletes reported hot flushes. What limits using this as the rate for all female endurance athletes aged 40–60?

options.text: Self-selected respondents and self-reported symptoms
options.why: Right: those with symptoms may be likelier to answer, which can bias the rate.

options.text: It asked about symptoms but not about training
options.why: It asked how symptoms affect training too; the limit is who chose to reply.

options.text: Hot flushes cannot be asked about online
options.why: Nothing stops questionnaires on symptoms; the issue is who replied.

options.text: The survey used a randomised control group
options.why: It was a cross-sectional survey with no control group.

variants.stem: Why can no one yet say which training type best prevents bone loss across the menopause transition?

options.text: Few trials, low quality, and few in perimenopausal women
options.why: Right: six low-quality trials, only two in perimenopause.

options.text: Training has been shown not to affect bone
options.why: Strength training and walking helped bone in early post-menopause.

options.text: Every trial found the same result
options.why: The trials differed by exercise type and stage.

options.text: Bone density cannot be measured
options.why: Trials measured it; there were simply too few good ones.
